paragraphs.title: The definition in one sentence
paragraphs.p: The limit of f(x) as x\to a is L if every output window around L contains all nearby values f(x), once x is restricted to a small enough punctured input window around a.

statement.p: The letter \delta is an allowed input error: a response, not a challenge. In your own words, why does the order first \varepsilon, then \delta matter, and what does a successful \delta guarantee about nearby outputs?

hint.p: You do not get to name the output tolerance. You only get to name how close the input must be. Once 0<|x-a|<\delta, the outputs must all lie inside the chosen \varepsilon-window around L.

exercise.title: How does the picture match the definition?

statement.p: The definition says that every horizontal band around L must contain the graph over some punctured vertical strip around a. In your own words, why does a jump fail this picture, and why can one-sided versions still succeed when the two-sided test fails?

hint.p: A two-sided strip has to control both sides at once. If the two sides head toward different heights, no single band around one target can hold both nearby pieces. A one-sided test only looks at one half of the strip.

subsection.title: What the definition gives us
subsection.p: The precise definition is not meant to replace intuition. It protects intuition.

It explains why a table can suggest a limit but not prove it. It explains why the value at the point may not matter. It explains why a jump breaks a two-sided limit. It gives us a way to prove limit laws instead of trusting them from graphs.
Most of the time, we will calculate limits using algebra, known limit laws, and continuity. But the \varepsilon-\delta definition is the foundation underneath those shortcuts.

note.title: What a finite limit really says
note.p: means that output error can be forced below any chosen tolerance by making input error small enough, while not requiring x=a.

subsection.p: Now that limits have a precise meaning, we can define a special kind of well-behaved function. It is the case where the nearby limit and the actual value agree. That property is called continuity, and it is the reason many familiar graphs can be drawn without lifting the pencil.
